Decontamination

Resources for assessing patient decontamination requirements, prioritizing patients, and conducting patient decontamination

Decontamination is the process of removing or neutralizing a chemical that is on a patient's body or clothing to stop the exposure and prevent further harm. For most toxic chemicals, decontamination is a first line treatment that should be performed as soon as possible since removing or neutralizing chemicals on the patient's body or clothing reduces the time they are exposed to the chemical. Decontamination will typically reduce the overall severity of symptoms the patient will experience.

In the first Few, Critical Minutes

Decontaminating patients as soon as possible increases survivability and potentially decreases adverse heath effects of contaminants.

  • Be aware of secondary contamination impacts. Contact with contaminated patients could expose others if not properly decontaminated.

Evacuate to safe distance before:

1
Emergency Self-Decon

  • Disrobe
  • Patients remove visible contamination from themselves
  • Use available materials

2
Gross Decon

  • Ladder-Pipe System (LPS) or alternate means of wet decontamination
  • Active Drying

3
Technical Decon

  • Contamination reduction to level as low as possible
  • Well-defined, multi-step process

Response Decontamination Guidances

Select the preferred patient decontamination guidance

 PRISM GUIDANCE

The Primary Response Incident Scene Management (PRISM) guidance, first published in 2015 and updated in 2018, was written to provide authoritative, evidence-based guidance on mass patient disrobe and decontamination during a chemical incident.
Remove up to 99.9% of contaminant by following the Triple Protocol

View PRISM Guidance (HHS/BARDA, 2018)

Flowchart to identify the most appropriate form of emergency decontamination. Dry decontamination methods should be the default option unless contaminate is a particulate (e.g. powder) and/or caustic.

Select patient decontamination methods based on available resources, weather conditions, and type of contaminant

Be prepared: Requires at least 4+ or more absorbent materials (pads, dressings, towels, etc.) per patient

  • Preferred method for Emergency Decontamination
  • Preferred method for cold weather conditions
  • Not for use when contaminant is a powder or other solid material or caustic material

Dry Emergency patient decontamination options

  • Dry absorbent materials

Examples include:

  • Wound care pack dressing swabs
  • Absorbent wound dressing
  • Wound care pack dressing swabs
  • Cotton wool
  • Wound dressing pad
  • Diaper
  • Spill pads
  • Paper towels
  • Bath towels

Wet Emergency Patient Decontamination

  • Wet emergency decontamination should only be performed when dry methods are contraindicated. That is, for caustic or corrosive chemicals (indicated by burning or painful skin) or non-liquid (powder or particulate) chemical contaminants. There is no quantitative evidence available for recommending a specific emergency wet decontamination protocol.
  • Use water source that is immediately available
    • Nearby spigot or faucet
    • Bottled water
    • Nearby water fountain
  • Alternatively, use any safe liquid
    • Soft drinks, juices, iced tea, lukewarm tea/coffee

Flowchart provides guidance for determining if gross decon may or may not be needed. Include professional judgment and scene-specific indicators to inform decision, as well.

If you'd like more information about determining the need for gross decontamination see the ASPIRE tool

Category Definition Decontamination Pathway
C1
Ambulatory 		Patients who are able to understand instructions and perform activities without assistance C1 - Standard
C2
Communications challenged 		Patients who are either unable to understand instructions or unable to perform actives without accommodations or assistance C2 - Standard or Non-ambulatory
C3
Non-ambulatory 		Patients who are unresponsive, have life-threatening injuries or require extensive accommodations or assistance C3 - Non-ambulatory

C1 - Ambulatory

Patients who are able to understand instructions and perform activities without assistance

C1 - Standard

C2 - Communications challenged

Patients who are either unable to understand instructions or unable to perform actives without accommodations or assistance

C2 - Standard or Non-ambulatory

C3 - Non-ambulatory

Patients who are unresponsive, have life-threatening injuries or require extensive accommodations or assistance

C3 - Non-ambulatory

Ambulatory patients process through all tiers of the decontamination process through Standard (Ambulatory) Response Pathway with or without assistance from first responders

Communications challenged patients process through either the Standard Response Pathway or Non-ambulatory Response Pathway depending on

  • Number of appropriately equipped first responders
  • Availability of technical decontamination units
  • Degree of assistance or accommodation required by each C2 - Communications challenged patient

Non-ambulatory patients process through all tiers of the decontamination process through a Non-ambulatory Response Pathway with a greater degree first responder intervention

CATEGORIZATION

All patient decontamination begins with evacuation of patients away and upwind from the hazardous area to a safer location for decontamination.

Evacuation is followed by disrobing. No form of decontamination should be undertaken before disrobing.

The “Triple Protocol” of sequentially conducting  each tier as one continuous process provides the most benefit to the patients. Select patient decontamination tier based on available resources, personnel, and time required to set up more advanced tiers.

Do not delay patient decontamination to wait for set up of more advanced tier.

For all patient decontamination tiers, consider patient privacy and modesty. Provide a means to minimize viewing by non-essential personnel. Separate males and females, if possible, during decontamination processes, but keep families together.

Actions patients can perform for themselves:

  • Remove clothing (reduces majority of contamination)
  • Use dry absorbent materials for patient self-care decontamination unless contaminant is corrosive or in powder form
  • Using available dry absorbent material on hair and top of head, blot for 10 seconds and rub for 10 seconds, and then the rest of the body working downwards (10:10)
  • Focus on compliant patients before dealing with those who refuse to cooperate
  • Collect used dry absorbent materials and dispose of as hazardous waste
  • Track patients’ personal items as best possible to enable decontamination and return later

See Determining the Need for Gross (wet) Decontamination and apply professional judgment in deciding if these steps are necessary

Ladder Pipe System (LPS)

  • Parallel park two fire engines to form a corridor through which patients pass while being sprayed with a high volume of low-pressure water mist
    • Alternative method: spray directly with hosepipe and fogging nozzle
  • Patients rub themselves from top to bottom, concentrating on areas most likely contaminated (hair/head, face, neck, and hands)
  • Patients should remain in LPS corridor for 15 to 30 seconds, but not longer to avoid "wash-in" effect.
  • Focus on compliant patients before dealing with individual who refuse to cooperate

Active Drying:

  • Patients use towels or other absorbent material to self-dry from top to bottom following completion of LPS
  • Collect used towels or absorbent material and dispose of as hazardous waste

Current Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) guidance suggests decontamination performed for lifesaving operations takes precedence over containment or on-site treatment of water run-off.

Note: the synergistic clinical benefits of the Triple Protocol are best accomplished when all three stages are performed as one continuous process

Determining the Need for Gross (Wet) Decontamination also applies to the Technical Decontamination stage

  • Usually performed by specialist decontamination unit and associated resources
  • Shower water should be between 95-104 F
  • Duration of 60-90 seconds for each patient
  • Addition of mild detergent to shower water
  • Use a new washcloth for each patient
  • Wash from head to toe
  • Non-ambulatory response pathway should include roller table for backboards
  • Focus on compliant patients before dealing with individual who refuse to cooperate
  • Active Drying: Patients should use towels or other absorbent material to self-dry from top to bottom following completion of Technical Decontamination
  • Collect used towels or absorbent material and dispose of as hazardous waste

Note: the synergistic clinical benefits of the Triple Protocol are best accomplished when all three stages are performed as one continuous process

  • Transfer limited mobility patients to backboard or gurney and treat as non-ambulatory
  • Enable patients to retain medical equipment (eyeglasses, hearing aids, prosthetics, etc.) as much as possible

  • Prioritize infants and children for decontamination
  • Consider psychological needs of children
  • Group children by gender and provide same-gender first responders to assist with disrobing
  • First responders should carry children not old enough to walk on a stretcher
    • Infants and young children should be carried in a laundry basket or baby bath by first responders and caregivers
  • Communicate with cartoons, posters, videos, and picture instructions as needed, if available

  • Prioritize pregnant patients for decontamination
  • Transfer limited mobility patients to backboard or gurney and treat as non-ambulatory

  • Transfer limited mobility patients to backboard or gurney and treat as non-ambulatory
  • Enable patients to retain medical equipment (eyeglasses, hearing aids, prosthetics, etc.) as much as possible
  • Include animal triage and decontamination for service animals
    • If able, service animals should stay with their handler throughout the decontamination process.

  • Provide written and photographic instructions for each step of each patient decontamination tier
  • Use verbal and sign-language interpreters
  • Include prerecorded instructions in different languages

  • Account for the handling of weapons
  • Law enforcement first responders collect, decontaminate, and maintain weapons for fellow law enforcement officers

Patient Decontamination National Planning Guidance

The Patient Decontamination National Planning Guidance, published in 2014, provides principles set forth from a strategic perspective to guide, but not specify operational practices. The guidance is evidence-based to the extent possible and provides sources when possible.

View Patient Decontamination in a Mass Chemical Exposure Incident: National Planning Guidance for Communities (DHS/HHS, 2014)

Note: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has archived this content as it may contain outdated information that may not reflect current policy or programs.

If the answer to one or more of the questions below is "yes", patient decontamination is recommended:

  • Have incident response teams indicated (signs, placards, credible witness, etc.) or detected (detection equipment) the presence of a chemical involved in the incident?
  • Are there obvious patient signs and symptoms of exposure?
  • Is there visible contamination on patients?
  • Were patients in close proximity to the release or dissemination location of a known or suspected chemical?
  • Are any patients requesting decontamination?

Prioritize patients by estimating relative risk and grouping patients into urgent and non-urgent groups. For mass decontamination, do the greatest good for the greatest number of patients.

Considerations:

  • Separate Ambulatory and non-ambulatory patients for processing through appropriately dedicated patient decontamination lanes to maximize throughput in each lane
  • Children should be prioritized before adults within the same group – and keep families together
  • Consider age, pregnancy, and chronic medical conditions
  • Concerned nearby personnel deemed unexposed to chemicals, but who request decontamination should be allowed, but are lowest priority

Select patient decontamination methods based on available resources, weather conditions, and type of containment

  • Preferred method for cold weather conditions
  • Not for use when contaminant is a powder or other solid material

Dry patient decontamination options

  • Dry particulate material

    Examples include:

  • Baking powder
  • Baking flour
  • Kitty Litter
  • Fuller’s Earth

Follow dry particulate material decontamination with wet method to remove particulate material

  • Dry absorbent materials

    Examples include:

  • Absorbent wound dressing
  • Spill Pads
  • Paper Towels
  • Bath Towels

  • Preferred method when gross and/or technical patient decontamination is deemed appropriate
  • Required method when contaminant is a powder or other solid material
  • Wet patient decontamination considerations
  • Recommended water pressure: 50 – 60 psi
  • Recommended water temperature: tepid
  • Mild soap suitable for skin contact, if available, should be added to water
  • Use non-abrasive sponge, washcloth, or similar wash item for light rubbing (do not reuse)
  • Do not delay patient decontamination to acquire additional resources
  • Current Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) guidance suggests decontamination performed for lifesaving operations takes precedence over containment or on-site treatment of water run-off.

  • Preferred method for specific contaminants
  • For Chemical Warfare Agents (CWA)- Spot decontamination with Reactive Skin Decontamination Lotion (RSDL) or other approved lotion/solution, if available
  • For phenolic compounds (for example, phenol resin or cresols) - Polyethylene glycol (PEG)

Select patient decontamination tier based on available resources, personnel, and time required to set up more advanced tiers.

The tiers are not necessarily a sequential process. Apply in a manner that meets the needs of each specific situation.

Each tier may be performed at incident scenes or at a health care facility. Ambulatory patients may leave the scene prior to decontamination and self-present at health care facilities.

Do not delay patient decontamination to wait for set up of more advanced tier.

For all patient decontamination tiers, consider patient privacy and modesty. Provide a means to minimize viewing by non-essential personnel. Separate males and females, if possible, during decontamination processes, but keep families together.

Actions patients can perform for themselves.

Goal: Hasty reduction of contamination with available resources as soon as possible after contamination occurred.

Advise patients to:

  • Distance themselves from site of chemical release/exposure
  • Remove clothing (reduces majority of contamination)
  • Wipe visible contamination from skin
  • Use available dry particulate materials (baking flour, kitty litter, etc.) or dry absorbent materials (wound dressing, towels, spill pads, etc.)
  • Track patients’ personal items as best possible to enable decontamination and return later

Non-ambulatory and some ambulatory patients may not be able to perform Self-Care Decontamination

Actions typically performed by first responders and first receivers.

Goal: Rapid and substantial reduction of contamination immediately after exposure.
Decontamination Procedure:

  • Use a Ladder Pipe System (LPS) with firefighting equipment to deliver a high-volume, low-pressure water shower.
  • If LPS is unavailable, provide alternative methods for high-volume, low-pressure water showers.
  • Conduct spot decontamination with Reactive Skin Decontamination Lotion (RSDL) for chemical warfare agent exposure.
  • Non-ambulatory patients and ambulatory patients requiring assistance should be supported throughout the decontamination process.

Planned and systematic actions, likely to be performed under the guidance of, or with the assistance of first responders or first receivers.

Goal: Achieve contamination reduction to a level that is as low as possible.

Setup:

  • Well-defined, multi-step process, usually with a mass patient decontamination infrastructure
  • Usually involves:
    • High-volume, low-pressure water shower
    • Addition of a mild soap (meant for skin contact)
    • Gentle rubbing with a soft cloth or sponge

Separate lanes for:

  • Ambulatory patients to walk through and follow directions at each step
  • Non-ambulatory patents on stretchers/litters to go through on roller table

  • Transfer limited mobility patients to backboard or gurney and treat as non-ambulatory
  • Enable patients to retain medical equipment (eyeglasses, hearing aids, prosthetics, etc.) as much as possible

  • Prioritize infants and children for decontamination
  • Consider psychological needs of children
  • Group children by gender and provide same-gender first responders to assist with disrobing
  • First responders should carry children not old enough to walk on a stretcher
    • Infants and young children should be carried in a laundry basket or baby bath by first responders and caregivers
  • Communicate with cartoons, posters, videos, and picture instructions as needed, if available

  • Prioritize pregnant patients for decontamination
  • Transfer limited mobility patients to backboard or gurney and treat as non-ambulatory

  • Transfer limited mobility patients to backboard or gurney and treat as non-ambulatory
  • Enable patients to retain medical equipment (eyeglasses, hearing aids, prosthetics, etc.) as much as possible
  • Include animal triage and decontamination for service animals
    • If able, service animals should stay with their handler throughout the decontamination process.

  • Provide written and photographic instructions for each step of each patient decontamination tier
  • Use verbal and sign-language interpreters
  • Include prerecorded instructions in different languages

  • Account for the handling of weapons
  • Law enforcement first responders collect, decontaminate, and maintain weapons for fellow law enforcement officers

Triple Protocol Stages

Emergency Self-Decontamination

Gross Decontamination

Technical Decontamination

Actions patients can perform for themselves.

  • Remove clothing (reduces majority of contamination)

  • Use dry absorbent materials for patient self-care decontamination unless contaminant is corrosive or in powder form

  • Using available dry absorbent material on hair and top of head, blot for 10 seconds and rub for 10 seconds (10:10)

  • Repeat 10:10 approach for face, then hands, then any other skin are not originally clothed

  • Focus on compliant patients before dealing with those who refuse to cooperate

  • Collect used dry absorbent materials and dispose of as hazardous waste

  • Track patients’ personal items as best possible to enable decontamination and return later

  • Focus on compliant patients before dealing with individual who refuse to cooperate

Active Drying:

  • Patients use towels or other absorbent material to self-dry from top to bottom following completion of LPS

  • Collect used towels or absorbent material and dispose of as hazardous waste

Current Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) guidance suggests decontamination performed for lifesaving operations takes precedence over containment or on-site treatment of water run-off.
